Multi-Task Particle Swarm Optimization with Knowledge-Guided Elite Refinement and Two-Phase Weight Scheduling for High-Dimensional Feature Selection Anonymous Author a a Anonymous Institution (masked for double-blind review), Abstract Feature selection in high-dimensional data remains a central challenge for evolutionary computation. Particle swarm optimization suffers from three structural deficiencies: random initialization provides insufficient guidance in sparse high-dimensional spaces, uniform mutation discards cross-iteration feature-importance signals, and static objective preferences cannot adapt to different evolutionary phases. To address these limitations, we propose KDS-EL (Knowledge-Guided Dual-Phase Swarm Evolutionary Learning), a closed-loop knowledge-guided evolutionary framework. First, to overcome cold-start inefficiency, we propose mutual-information-guided initialization with adaptive re-initialization, injecting prior knowledge and recovering population diversity when stagnation occurs. Second, to exploit discarded cross-iteration feature-importance signals, we propose a knowledge-guided elite refinement strategy that accumulates feature-importance knowledge and steers elite solutions toward historically effective features. Third, to align objective weights with search phases, we propose two-phase weight scheduling that emphasizes early dimensionality reduction and late-stage accuracy refinement. On 20 high-dimensional benchmarks, KDS-EL ranks first among all competitors, achieving a mean accuracy of 0.9574 with only 87.8 selected features, outperforming the strongest single- and multi-objective competitors by +3.97 and +4.42 percentage points; Wilcoxon and Holm–Bonferroni tests confirm statistically significant improvements over all 13 competitors. Keywords: feature selection, particle swarm optimization, mutual information, knowledge-guided elite refinement, two-phase weight scheduling 1. Introduction High-dimensional data have emerged as a fundamental challenge in clas- sification problems across diverse domains, including genomics, text mining, and computer vision. These datasets typically contain from hundreds to mil- lions of features, while only a limited number of labeled samples are available, resulting in the well-known p ≫ n scenario. Under such conditions, conven- tional learning algorithms often suffer from severe overfitting, increased com- putational complexity, and reduced interpretability due to the curse of dimen- sionality [1, 2]. Feature selection (FS) has therefore become an essential pre- processing technique that aims to identify a compact and informative subset of features while preserving classification performance. However, selecting an op- timal feature subset remains highly challenging because the search space grows exponentially with the number of features D, and FS is an NP-hard combinato- rial optimization problem [3]. Moreover, individual feature relevance measures are insufficient to characterize complex feature interactions and dependencies, which are often critical for achieving robust classification performance. FS methods are generally categorized into filter, wrapper, and embedded approaches [1, 4]. Filter methods rank features according to statistical criteria and offer high computational efficiency, but they usually evaluate features inde- pendently of the classifier and thus ignore classifier-specific relevance. Embed- ded methods incorporate feature selection into the learning process, providing a compromise between selection efficiency and predictive performance; however, their effectiveness is often dependent on the characteristics of specific learning models. Wrapper methods directly optimize feature subsets according to clas- sifier performance and can achieve competitive classification results, but the repeated model evaluations make them computationally expensive, especially in high-dimensional search spaces. To address the combinatorial complexity of wrapper-based FS, evolutionary computation has been extensively investigated as a promising optimization paradigm [5–7]. By maintaining a population of candidate solutions, evolutionary algorithms can perform global exploration of feature subsets without requiring gradient information. Among them, particle swarm optimization (PSO), genetic algorithms, and differential evolution have demonstrated promising results on high-dimensional FS tasks. PSO has become one of the most widely adopted evolutionary algorithms for FS due to its simple structure, efficient information-sharing mechanism, and fast convergence. Nevertheless, conventional PSO-based FS methods still encounter several structural limitations when dealing with sparse and high-dimensional search spaces. First, random initialization distributes particles without prior guidance throughout the binary search space, whereas effective feature subsets usually occupy only a small region with limited active dimensions. Consequently, a considerable number of fitness evaluations may be wasted on redundant and suboptimal solutions before the swarm identifies Email address: corresponding.author@example.com (Anonymous Author) promising search regions. Second, conventional uniform bit-flip mutation treats all dimensions equally and neglects the feature-level improvement information accumulated during previous evaluations, preventing the search from exploiting historically informative features. Third, existing PSO-based FS methods typically employ fixed objective weights to balance classification error and feature ratio during the entire optimization process. However, the desired trade-off between feature reduction and accuracy refinement varies across search stages: aggressive sparsity enhancement is preferred in early exploration, whereas accurate decision boundary refinement becomes more important after a compact subset has been obtained. Recent evolutionary FS studies have attempted to improve search perfor- mance through enhanced population initialization, adaptive evolutionary op- erators, and refined fitness evaluation strategies [8–11]. Although these ap- proaches have achieved promising results, they usually focus on isolated com- ponents of the optimization process and lack a unified mechanism for improv- ing early-stage exploration, exploiting historical feature information, and adapt- ing optimization objectives throughout evolution. Recently, multi-task PSO has emerged as an effective paradigm for high-dimensional FS with fixed-length binary representations. For instance, MEL [12] adopts cooperative subpopula- tions and a fixed-length binary encoding strategy to efficiently handle feature spaces containing tens of thousands of dimensions. Despite its effectiveness, existing multi-task PSO-based FS frameworks still leave several challenges un- resolved: the initial population is generally generated without sufficient feature- level prior knowledge, useful feature-importance information discovered during evolution is not explicitly retained and exploited, and the balance between clas- sification performance and feature sparsity remains unchanged across different search stages. To address these limitations, this paper proposes KDS-EL (Knowledge- Guided Dual-Phase Swarm Evolutionary Learning), a closed-loop knowledge- guided evolutionary framework that enables knowledge acquisition, accumula- tion, and exploitation throughout the multi-task PSO search process. The pro- posed framework integrates three complementary mechanisms that address dif- ferent stages of high-dimensional FS optimization. First, mutual-information-guided initialization with adaptive re- initialization incorporates prior feature-relevance knowledge into population construction and reduces the search waste caused by unguided initialization in the early stage. Second, the Knowledge-guided Elite Refinement (KER) strategy accumulates cross-iteration feature-importance knowledge from the fitness comparisons already performed during search, applies exponential decay to reduce the influence of outdated evidence, and guides elite solutions toward historically informative features within a bounded refinement budget. Third, Two-Phase Weight Scheduling dynamically adjusts the dual-objective preference from feature reduction to classification refinement, matching optimization priorities with the evolving requirements of high-dimensional FS. These mechanisms operate at complementary levels of the evolutionary process, and their individual contributions can be systematically verified through component contribution analysis. The main contributions of this paper are summarized as follows: 2.2. Single-Objective Evolutionary Feature Selection Evolutionary algorithms have been extensively applied to feature selec- tion for their population-based global search and gradient-free nature. Early work adapted classical meta-heuristics—binary PSO (BPSO) [7], ant colony optimization [21], artificial bee colony [22], and genetic algorithms with sup- port vector machines [23]—to the binary subset selection problem, establish- ing the template of a population of candidate subsets evolving under selection, crossover, and mutation guided by a scalar fitness function. Because standard evolutionary operators degrade at high dimensionality, specialized single-objective methods have been developed: self-adaptive PSO adjusting swarm size and mutation rate [24], progressively refined PSO al- ternating between coarse- and fine-grained search [25], and problem-specific heuristics—FWPSO [8], which biases velocity updates with per-feature im- portance; SaWDE [9] with adaptive weighting; IGPSO [10], which estimates relevance via a multi-layer perceptron; and PSO-CSM [11] integrating mul- tiple evaluation criteria. Learning-based control and space decomposition are also explored: reinforcement-learning-aided PSO [26] and divide-and-conquer search [27]. These methods refine search operators but do not systematically exploit accumulated feature-importance knowledge harvested from the search itself. 1. We propose an MI-guided initialization scheme with adaptive re-initialization, which incorporates feature-relevance knowledge into population construction and restores search diversity when evolutionary stagnation occurs. 2. We propose the Knowledge-guided Elite Refinement (KER) strategy, which accumulates cross-iteration feature-importance evidence from the fitness comparisons already performed during search, reduces the influence of obsolete knowledge through exponential decay, and per- forms knowledge-guided elite refinement within a bounded refinement budget. 3. We propose Two-Phase Weight Scheduling (TPS), which replaces static objective weighting with a dynamic optimization strategy consisting of an early feature-reduction phase and a later accuracy-refinement phase, thereby aligning optimization preferences with the temporal character- istics of high-dimensional FS. 4. We conduct comprehensive experiments on 20 high-dimensional benchmark datasets containing 500 to 54,675 features and compare KDS-EL with 14 fixed-length evolutionary FS methods. Extensive evaluations, including component contribution analysis and parameter sensitivity analysis, are performed to validate the effectiveness and robustness of the proposed framework. 2.3. Mutual-Information-Guided and Importance-Aware Evolutionary Meth- ods Extensive experiments demonstrate that KDS-EL achieves the best over- all performance, obtaining an average classification accuracy of 0.9574 with only 87.8 selected features. Compared with the strongest single-objective and multi-objective competitors, KDS-EL improves accuracy by 3.97 and 4.42 per- centage points, respectively, while achieving a 3.4× speedup over MEL (51.4 s vs. 175.0 s). Furthermore, Wilcoxon signed-rank tests with Holm–Bonferroni correction confirm that the improvements are statistically significant over all 13 competitors. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 reviews fea- ture selection methods and evolutionary FS algorithms. Section 3 introduces the background knowledge, including PSO, mutual-information-based feature relevance estimation, and the MEL framework. Section 4 presents the proposed KDS-EL framework and describes its three mechanisms in detail. Section 5 reports the experimental configuration and results, including comparative ex- periments, component contribution analysis, and parameter sensitivity analysis. Finally, Section 6 concludes this paper and discusses future research directions. Mutual information (MI) quantifies the reduction in label uncertainty pro- vided by a feature [28] and is the most widely used relevance score in hybrid filter-wrapper feature selection. In filter form, mRMR [15] and FCBF [16] rank features before any classifier is trained, offering efficient coarse pruning at the price of ignoring feature interactions, as discussed in Section 2.1. Within evo- lutionary wrappers, MI and related importance scores have also been used to shape the search itself: Yu et al. [29] rank features by MI and initialize a multi- population differential evolution with the top-ranked subset; FWPSO biases velocity updates with per-feature importance scores [8]; and IGPSO learns a feature-importance estimate with a multilayer perceptron [10]. These methods demonstrate that prior relevance knowledge can improve the starting point or update direction of evolutionary search. Such filter-driven schemes, however, consume the injected knowledge one-shot: MI rankings are computed before optimization and are never revised by the search itself. The per-feature evidence accumulated across iterations—which additions or removals improved fitness—is discarded, and subsequent operators remain uniform. KDS-EL instead treats feature- importance knowledge as an in-loop state: MI scores bootstrap the initial population, while the KER strategy maintains a cumulative feature-importance matrix that is updated from the fitness comparisons already performed during search and re-deployed to refine elite solutions within a bounded refinement budget. 2. Related Work 2.1. Feature Selection Paradigms Feature selection is a fundamental pre-processing step in high-dimensional data analysis, aiming to identify a minimal subset of relevant features that preserves or improves classification performance while reducing computational cost and enhancing interpretability [1, 2]. Methods fall broadly into three paradigms: filter, wrapper, and embedded. Filter methods evaluate features independently of any learning algorithm, relying on intrinsic data properties such as variance, correlation, or eigenvec- tor centrality [13, 14]. Representative techniques include the minimum Redun- dancy Maximum Relevance (mRMR) criterion [15] and the Fast Correlation- Based Filter (FCBF) [16]. These methods are computationally efficient and scale readily to high-dimensional settings, yet they disregard feature interac- tions and may retain redundant subsets under strong inter-feature correlation. Wrapper methods treat feature selection as a search problem, evaluating candidate subsets by the predictive performance of a specific classifier [4]. Hybrid genetic algorithms [17] and other meta-heuristic wrappers can capture complex feature interdependencies, but their computational cost grows rapidly with dimensionality, as each candidate subset requires a full classifier training- and-evaluation cycle. Embedded methods integrate feature selection into model training. Lasso and its bootstrapped variant Bolasso [18] enforce sparsity through L 1 regular- ization; gradient-boosting-based approaches such as FS-GBDT [19] leverage tree-split importance; and hybrid algorithms like ILRC [20] combine regular- ization with clustering. Embedded methods offer a favorable speed–accuracy trade-off, but their feature rankings are tied to specific model assumptions. At high dimensionality, each paradigm faces distinct structural bot- tlenecks: filters are fast but oblivious to feature interactions, wrappers are accurate but face a search space that grows exponentially with dimension, and embedded methods depend on model-specific regularization biases. These complementary weaknesses motivate evolutionary computation, which decouples the search mechanism from the evaluation metric and navigates the exploration–exploitation trade-off through population-based global search. 2.4. Multi-Objective Evolutionary Feature Selection Multi-objective feature selection (MOFS) treats classification accuracy and feature count as competing objectives, producing a Pareto front of non-dominated solutions. Xue et al. [30] pioneered multi-objective PSO for feature selection, showing that jointly optimizing accuracy and subset size yields more diverse and informative solutions than scalarized approaches. Hu et al. [31] extended this framework with fuzzy cost functions for imbalanced classification. The multi-objective evolutionary algorithm family provides several archi- tectures for this problem. NSGA-II-FS [32] uses non-dominated sorting and crowding distance to maintain Pareto-front diversity. MOEA/D-FS [33] de- composes the problem into scalar subproblems solved cooperatively. MOPSO- FS [34] extends single-objective PSO with an external archive and Pareto- dominance-based leader selection. Hancer et al. [35] combined evolutionary search with filter-based ranking under both single- and multi-objective settings. Despite their conceptual advantages, MOFS methods incur substantial overhead: maintaining an external archive, non-dominated sorting, and Pareto-front management all cost significant time (in our experiments, over 110 seconds on average). Moreover, under fixed-length binary encoding at high dimensionality, the Pareto front expands combinatorially and convergence slows, limiting scalability at gene-expression scale. Surrogate-assisted multi-objective search [36] can mitigate evaluation cost, yet surrogate accuracy and training overhead under extreme dimensionality remain open problems. KDS-EL therefore adopts the single-objective weighted formulation, which delivers a single compact solution directly, and retains MOFS methods only as comparison methods. 2 uniformly from [0, 1], and p best,i and g best denote the personal and global best positions, respectively. For feature selection, each candidate solution is a binary mask indicating whether a feature is selected. Evolutionary Multi-Task Learning Evolutionary multi-task learning solves multiple related tasks jointly, with knowledge transfer accelerating convergence. Zhang and Yang [37] surveyed the multi-task learning foundations on which such evolutionary approaches build, and several instantiations target feature selection: a minion-based mul- titasking framework [38], PSO-based multitasking for high-dimensional classi- fication [39, 40], multitask bee colony optimization for hyperspectral band se- lection [41], and multitasking for large-scale multi-objective optimization [42]. Of particular relevance to fixed-length high-dimensional feature selection, MEL [12] divides a PSO population into two subpopulations that cooperate through cross-task knowledge transfer, sharing feature-importance knowledge while searching independently, and provides the multi-task PSO framework on which KDS-EL builds in Section 4. KDS-EL, in contrast, binarizes continuous positions with the fixed threshold θ = 0.6 described in Section 4.2. In the p ≫ n regime, standard binary PSO converges slowly and tends toward premature stagnation, because the veloc- ity update provides no domain-grounded gradient toward sparse, high-accuracy regions. 2.6. Gene-Expression Feature Selection High-dimensional gene expression data present a particularly challenging testbed: the number of features routinely exceeds the number of samples by two to three orders of magnitude—a “small N, large D” regime where conventional statistical methods break down and overfitting is pervasive [43, 44]. Represen- tative applications include cancer staging [45], Alzheimer’s classification from neuroimaging features [46], biomarker gene identification [8], multi-cancer risk module discovery [19, 20], and surrogate-assisted multi-objective gene selec- tion from large-scale single-cell RNA sequencing data [47]. Two structural properties amplify the difficulty. First, feature redundancy is exceptionally high: co-regulated genes exhibit correlated expression, so dis- tinct subsets frequently yield near-identical accuracy. Second, a non-trivial frac- tion of gene datasets reach accuracy ceilings—exceeding 0.998 under multi- ple methods—rendering accuracy alone insufficient to distinguish algorithmic quality; on these datasets the selected feature count becomes the primary dis- criminatory metric. Evaluation must therefore jointly consider classification ac- curacy and subset compactness. Recent methodological development in this area is extensive; surveys of evolutionary computation for biomarker identification in complex diseases [3] and instance-selection-assisted evolutionary feature selection [48] both target the small-sample, ultra-high-dimensional regime central to gene-expression analysis. 3.2. Mutual-Information-Based Feature Filtering Mutual information measures the reduction in label uncertainty provided by a feature and is a standard filter score in high-dimensional feature selec- tion [15, 28, 49]. For a discrete feature f j and the class label Y, the mutual information is defined as I( f j ; Y) = p( f j = b, Y = c) log 2 b∈{0,1} c∈C p( f j = b, Y = c) , p( f j = b) p(Y = c) (3) where the sums run over the binary feature values and the class labels. Filtering by mutual information computes the score of every feature, ranks the features in descending order, and retains only a small fraction of the top-ranked dimensions before a classifier is trained. Algorithm 1 summarizes this procedure with a retention ratio k [49]; in high-dimensional gene-expression settings, retaining 2–5% of the features is typical. Algorithm 1 Feature filtering based on mutual information Require: Training dataset Ω, feature count p, class labels Y, retention ratio k Ensure: Filtered feature set S MI 1: S MI ← ∅ 2: for i = 1 to p do 3: Compute the mutual information I( f i ; Y) ▷ (3) 4: end for 5: Sort features by descending MI score and store the ranked indices in IDX 6: S MI ← the top ⌊p · k⌋ features of IDX 7: return S MI 2.7. Positioning of KDS-EL Across the evolutionary feature selection literature reviewed above, three gaps recur in high-dimensional feature selection. First, initialization is typically random, wasting a large fraction of the evaluation budget in a sparse search space. Second, search operators treat all dimensions uniformly and discard the cross-iteration evidence of which features have improved fitness. Third, the ob- jective weights balancing accuracy against subset size remain fixed throughout search, although feature selection has a natural temporal structure: noise elimi- nation is best performed early, and accuracy refinement late. KDS-EL addresses these gaps as a closed-loop knowledge-guided evolu- tionary framework built upon the multi-task PSO architecture of MEL [12]. Mutual-information-guided initialization with adaptive re-initialization injects prior feature-relevance knowledge at the outset; the KER strategy accumulates a feature-importance matrix from the fitness comparisons already performed dur- ing search, discounts obsolete evidence by exponential decay, and flips elite so- lutions toward effective features within a bounded refinement budget; and Two- Phase Weight Scheduling aligns the objective weights with a reduction-then- refinement schedule. The fixed-length encoding inherited from MEL keeps the framework efficient at tens of thousands of dimensions, and each mechanism is independently verifiable through the component contribution analysis in Sec- tion 5.8. KDS-EL does not hard-prune the search space with this filter. Instead, Sec- tion 4.2 reuses the same MI ranking to seed the initial population, preserving the full feature space while transferring the filter’s knowledge into the evolutionary loop. 3.3. Multi-Task Evolutionary Learning MEL [12] is a PSO-based multi-task evolutionary learning method for high-dimensional feature selection. Its population of N particles is divided into two equal-sized subpopulations, Sub 1 and Sub 2, each searching for an optimal feature subset with a distinct strategy. All particles share the same fixed-length real-valued representation, and a threshold θ converts each position into the bi- nary decision of whether a feature is selected. The two subpopulations share a feature-importance matrix W ∈ R D as the knowledge state of the search. Ini- tially zero, W is updated after each generation from the accuracy change of every particle: when the accuracy of a particle improves, the importance scores of features newly selected by that particle increase and the importance scores of discarded features decrease by the same amount, with the opposite adjustment when accuracy declines. Knowledge transfer connects the two tasks in complementary directions. Sub 1 follows the standard PSO update with an additional learning term, namely the best solution of Sub 2, so the experience of the second subpopulation guides the first. Sub 2 exploits the learned weights directly, excluding features with non-positive weights and selecting each remaining feature with probability pro- portional to its weight. The two subpopulations therefore search independently while continuously sharing feature-importance knowledge across tasks. KDS-EL inherits three elements of MEL. First, the fixed-length binary de- cision vector is shared by all components of Section 4. Second, the scalar fit- ness with which MEL maintains personal, subpopulation, and global bests is 3. Third, the fitness function of MEL is a weighted sum of classification error and subset sparsity:  ∥x∥ 0 , f (x) = α · 1 − Acc(x) + β · D (4) where Acc(x) is the k-nearest-neighbor accuracy of the selected features, ∥x∥ 0 is the number of selected features, and α = 0.9 and β = 0.1 are fixed weights [12]. Since both weights remain constant throughout search, MEL cannot adapt its objective emphasis to the temporal structure of feature selection, and Section 4 replaces this static weighting with Two-Phase Weight Scheduling. The domi- nant per-generation cost of MEL is the evaluation of the N particles, each re- quiring KNN-based five-fold cross-validation, giving an overall complexity of O(T · N · T eval ). 4.2. MI-guided Initialization and Adaptive Re-initialization To overcome the cold-start inefficiency of random initialization in sparse high-dimensional search spaces, we propose an MI-guided initialization with adaptive re-initialization that seeds the initial population with feature-quality information derived from mutual information. Random initialization typically produces individuals with approximately half of the features active, far from the sparse configurations that characterize effective feature subsets, wasting a substantial fraction of the fixed evaluation budget on low-quality regions; the adaptive re-initialization restarts stagnated individuals with informed seeds. Following the filter formulation of Section 3.2, all D features are ranked by descending MI score. With MI_init_ratio = 0.5, half of the initial population is seeded from the normalized MI score vector perturbed by small Gaussian noise, while the other half is initialized with uniform random positions. The resulting continuous position values are binarized with the fixed threshold θ = 0.6, i.e., a feature is selected when its position value exceeds θ. This balanced design ensures that half the population inherits prior feature-quality knowledge while the other half maintains the exploratory coverage of random seeding. Algorithm 2 summarizes this hybrid initialization procedure. 4. Proposed KDS-EL Algorithm 4.1. Overall Framework KDS-EL is a dual-subpopulation evolutionary algorithm integrating three complementary mechanisms within the multi-task particle swarm optimization framework of MEL [12]. Figure 1 shows the complete pipeline transform- ing raw high-dimensional data into a compact, high-accuracy feature subset through knowledge-guided operations. The algorithm takes as input a dataset with D features and C classes. In the preprocessing stage, mutual information between each feature and the class label is computed to produce a quality ranking over all D dimensions, as de- tailed in Section 4.2. An initial population of N fixed-length binary individuals is then constructed by mixing MI-ranked seeds with randomly initialized indi- viduals at a controlled ratio MI_init_ratio = 0.5, followed by binarization with the fixed threshold θ = 0.6. This hybrid scheme supplies a quality-informed starting point while preserving the diversity necessary for effective exploration. The population enters the main iterative loop. Each generation opens with dual-objective fitness evaluation under the Two-Phase Weight Scheduling weights defined in Section 4.5. Observed improvements update the cumulative feature-importance matrix W ∈ R D with exponential decay γ = 0.99, maintained as in Section 4.3. The top elite_k = 3 individuals are refined by the KER strategy of Section 4.4—a knowledge-guided flip mechanism with a 90%/10% knowledge-to-random split—and the population then undergoes the framework’s dual-subpopulation update: Sub 1 follows the PSO rule with an additional attractor toward Sub 2’s best, while Sub 2 samples features according to the cumulative importance matrix W. The importance matrix W is the sole knowledge state maintained by KDS-EL across iterations; all KER decisions rely exclusively on its relative ordering. This distinguishes W from the feature-importance matrix of MEL: MEL learns importance scores from per-generation accuracy changes and uses them to bias the probabilistic selection of one subpopulation, whereas KDS-EL discounts the accumulated evidence with exponential decay and re-deploys it through deterministic, budget-bounded flips on elite solutions. To further guard against premature convergence, KDS-EL incorporates an adaptive MI re-initialization loop. When the global-best fitness stagnates for stall_patience = 20 consecutive generations, the lower-performing half of the population is re-seeded with MI-informed positions—the precomputed feature- quality scores perturbed by small Gaussian noise—and re-evaluated under the current objective weights. This restores diversity with feature-quality guidance, allowing the population to escape local optima that trap static-initialization al- gorithms. Algorithm 3 summarizes this procedure. Knowledge-guided Elite Refinement Strategy To exploit the cross-iteration feature-importance signals discarded by uniform mutation, we propose the KER strategy, which injects population- accumulated feature importance into elite solutions through a bounded, knowledge-guided perturbation. It operates once per generation, after fitness evaluation and importance-matrix update, and targets only the top elite_k = 3 individuals selected by fitness rank; each refined elite is re-evaluated immediately and retained only if it improves fitness. For each elite individual x ∈ {0, 1} D , a probabilistic branching decision is made. With probability rand_flip_p = 0.10, the individual enters a pure ran- dom exploration branch: ⌊ϕD⌋ randomly selected features are toggled, where ϕ = flip_frac = 0.01. This branch guarantees ergodicity and prevents the search from locking onto stale or misleading importance accumulations. With proba- bility 1 − rand_flip_p = 0.90, the individual enters the knowledge-driven refine- ment branch. Each feature j is assigned the flip score    if x j = 0,  W j , σ j =    −W j , if x j = 1, MI-guided initialization is a well-established filter-wrapper technique in the feature selection literature [15, 28]. It provides the foundational quality layer upon which the subsequent knowledge-accumulation and scheduling mechanisms build. 4.3. Cumulative Feature-Importance Matrix with Exponential Decay To preserve the cross-iteration feature-importance signals discarded by uniform mutation, KDS-EL maintains a cumulative feature-importance matrix W ∈ R D , initialized to the zero vector, that aggregates these signals across it- erations. This matrix serves as the knowledge substrate for the KER strategy described in Section 4.4. After each generation’s fitness evaluation, the importance matrix is up- dated from every evaluated candidate whose fitness improves over its personal best. Let C i be the set of features whose selection status changed for individual pbest i, and let δ i = f i − f i new > 0 be the improvement magnitude. The update rule is W j ← W j + δ i · (2x i j − 1), j ∈ C i , (5) so that absent high-importance features and present low-importance features re- ceive the largest scores. Let S contain the ⌊ϕD⌋ features with the largest scores. The refined binary vector x ′ is then:     1 − x j , if j ∈ S, x ′ j =  (7)   x j , otherwise. The two refinement branches are illustrated in Figure 3: the knowledge- driven branch flips the ⌊ϕD⌋ highest-scoring features according to the impor- tance matrix W, while the random branch flips the same number of uniformly selected bits; both branches re-evaluate the refined elite and retain it only when fitness improves. where x i j ∈ {0, 1} is the selection status of feature j in the improved candidate. Algorithm 6 summarizes this schedule. Algorithm 6 Two-Phase Weight Scheduling Require: Generation index t, total generations T , split ratio α = PhaseSplit = 0.7 Ensure: Dual-objective weight vector w(t) 1: if t ≤ αT then 2: w(t) ← [0.7, 0.3] ▷ Phase 1: aggressive feature reduction 3: else 4: w(t) ← [0.95, 0.05] ▷ Phase 2: accuracy refinement 5: end if 6: return w(t) Re-evaluate; keep only if f improves Figure 3: KER strategy: for each top-3 elite, the flip direction is determined by the cumulative importance matrix W with probability p = 0.9, or by uniform random bit selection with probability p = 0.1; refined elites are re-evaluated and kept only on improvement. The intuition behind (7) is straightforward: the cumulative importance ma- trix W encodes which features have been consistently correlated with fitness improvements. High-importance features absent from an elite are candidates for inclusion; low-importance features still present are candidates for removal. The flip fraction ϕ = 0.01 is deliberately small—roughly one feature per hundred dimensions—so KER performs targeted local refinement rather than disruptive mutation. Crucially, acquiring the knowledge itself does not enlarge the evalu- ation budget: the importance matrix is updated from the fitness improvements already computed for the population. KER spends only a bounded refinement budget—re-evaluating the top elite_k = 3 elites per generation—which does not alter the dominant per-iteration complexity, since KNN cross-validation dominates and elite_k ≪ N. This reuse of accumulated feature-level knowl- edge at bounded cost distinguishes KER from recent knowledge-guided meta- heuristics [50]; the full refinement procedure is consolidated in Algorithm 5. In Phase 1 (t ≤ 0.7T ), the heavier feature-ratio penalty w f = 0.3 drives rapid elimination of irrelevant and redundant features, reducing the search from thousands of dimensions to dozens. In Phase 2 (t > 0.7T ), the weight prioritizes classification accuracy (w a = 0.95), enabling fine-grained refinement over the surviving compact subset. This coarse-to-fine design contrasts with the fixed w = [0.9, 0.1] of KDS-EL w/o TPS: a constant weight cannot simultaneously deliver aggressive early feature reduction and precise late-stage accuracy tun- ing. Time-varying search parameters are a general PSO principle, most notably the linearly decreasing inertia weight of [6] [5]. KDS-EL employs an in-place update: after KER refinement, each elite’s refined vector overwrites its original within the population when it improves fit- ness; no auxiliary pool is maintained, so the candidate set never expands to 2N. This simplifies the architecture and yields a measurable speed improvement, as analyzed in Section 4.7, without sacrificing quality—KDS-EL w/o TPS already surpasses MEL by +6.20 pp. Algorithm 5 Knowledge-guided Elite Refinement Require: Elite solution x e , feature-importance matrix W, flip fraction ϕ = flip_frac, random-flip probability p = rand_flip_p, fitness function f ⋆ Ensure: Refined elite x ⋆ e with f (x e ) ≤ f (x e ) 1: if rand() < p then 2: Select ⌊ϕD⌋ features uniformly at random 3: x ′ ← flip the selected bits of x e 4: else 5: Assign each feature j the score σ j = W j if x e, j = 0, else σ j = −W j 6: Select the ⌊ϕD⌋ highest-scoring features 7: x ′ ← flip the selected bits of x e 8: end if 9: Evaluate f (x ′ ) under current weights ▷ (9) 10: if f (x ′ ) < f (x e ) then ′ 11: x ⋆ e ← x 12: else 13: x ⋆ e ← x e 14: end if 15: return x ⋆ e 4.6. Main Algorithm and Pseudocode Algorithm 7 presents the complete KDS-EL procedure, consolidating the initialization and main loop; Algorithms 2, 3, 4, 5, and 6 detail the initialization, re-initialization, knowledge-update, refinement, and scheduling procedures it invokes. The algorithm computes MI scores and generates a hybrid initial popu- lation, then runs T = 100 generations of phase-dependent fitness evaluation, importance-matrix update with decay, KER refinement of the top three elites via Algorithm 5, and the dual-subpopulation update in which Sub 1 follows the PSO rule and Sub 2 samples features by importance-guided selection. Stagna- tion triggers adaptive MI re-initialization via Algorithm 3, and the best encod- ing is returned as the feature subset. 4.7. Complexity Analysis The computational cost of KDS-EL decomposes into a one-time initial- ization cost and per-iteration costs. The initial MI ranking requires comput- ing I( f j ; Y) for all D features and sorting the scores, costing O(D log D). Each generation incurs: (a) fitness evaluation over N individuals with KNN classi- fication, O(N · T eval ), where T eval dominates all other per-iteration operations; (b) importance-matrix update from fitness improvements, O(N · D); (c) elite se- lection and KER refinement (sorting D importance scores, flipping ϕD features, and re-evaluating the elite_k refined elites), O(elite_k · (D + T eval )). The adap- tive MI re-initialization executes only on stagnation, contributing an amortized O(D) per iteration. Collecting terms, the total complexity is: 4.5. Two-Phase Weight Scheduling Strategy To align objective weights with the temporal structure of feature selec- tion, we propose a Two-Phase Weight Scheduling strategy that replaces fixed objective weights with an early feature-reduction phase and a late accuracy- refinement phase. Conventional PSO-based feature selection methods employ fixed objective weights throughout the entire search, typically balancing clas- sification error and feature ratio with a static weighting such as w = [0.9, 0.1]. This rigid scheduling fails to exploit a structural property of the feature se- lection problem: noise-feature elimination is a one-time cost best handled ag- gressively at the outset, whereas accuracy refinement benefits from sustained fine-tuning over a compact, already-pruned feature set. A single fixed weight vector must compromise between these two temporally distinct demands. KDS-EL resolves this tension through a Two-Phase Weight Scheduling strategy. The total T iterations are partitioned by a split point at αT , where α = PhaseSplit = 0.7. The dual-objective weight vector w(t) = [w a (t), w f (t)] follows a step schedule:      [0.7, 0.3], w(t) =     [0.95, 0.05], (9) t ≤ αT (Phase 1: aggressive feature reduction), t > αT (Phase 2: accuracy refinement).  O D log D + T · (N · T eval + N · D + elite_k · (D + T eval )) . (10) MEL [12] has complexity O(T · N · T eval ). The added O(N · D + elite_k · (D + T eval )) per generation is bounded relative to O(N · T eval ), since elite_k = 3 ≪ N = 20 and KNN cross-validation T eval dominates. Empirically, KDS-EL completes in 51.4 s versus 175.0 s for MEL (3.4× speedup), confirming that the sparser subsets promoted by the knowledge-guided mechanisms shorten each evaluation and more than offset the marginal overhead. Table 1 maps methods to references. All comparison methods use the hyper-parameters recommended in their original publications, retaining default values where a parameter is un- specified. All methods share a unified configuration. A K-nearest neighbor (KNN) classifier with k = 3 serves as the base evaluator, with accuracy estimated via stratified 5-fold cross-validation with random shuffling. All algorithms use N = 20 candidate solutions and T = 100 iterations, and methods relying on continuous-to-binary mapping use threshold θ = 0.6. Every experiment is re- peated across 10 independent runs without fixing random seeds, letting the random-number generator flow naturally between runs. The KDS-EL parameter set is: knowledge weight decay WeightDecay = 0.99; phase split PhaseSplit = 0.7 with objective weights w s = [0.7, 0.3] (Phase 1, feature reduction) and w s = [0.95, 0.05] (Phase 2, refinement); KER flip fraction flip_frac = 0.01; random exploration probability rand_flip_p = 0.10; MI-init ratio MI_init_ratio = 0.5; elite count elite_k = 3; and stall patience stall_patience = 20 for adaptive MI re-initialization. Table 3 summarizes these settings. Experiments run on a desk- top workstation with an Intel i5-13700KF CPU and 32 GB RAM. For each method and dataset we report classification accuracy (mean and standard deviation over 10 runs), the number of selected features with its selec- tion ratio, and runtime in seconds. Statistical significance follows the protocol of Demšar [52]: the Friedman rank test [53] on the 20-dataset accuracy ma- trix detects overall differences; pairwise one-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank tests (p < 0.05) compare KDS-EL with each of the 13 methods in the direction of superiority; and the resulting p-values are Holm–Bonferroni corrected [54] to control the family-wise error rate. This standard protocol establishes whether observed differences are statistically meaningful rather than artifacts of finite experimental repetition. Following the table convention of [49], Table 4 additionally annotates ev- ery competitor cell with +, ≈, or − from a two-sided Wilcoxon rank-sum test (p < 0.05) over the 10 independent runs of that dataset. The symbols indicate that KDS-EL is significantly better than, statistically indistinguishable from, or significantly worse than the column method, respectively, on the corresponding dataset. 5. Experimental Results and Analysis Table 1: The 14 fixed-length methods compared in this study. Method Category Reference KDS-EL Proposed This work KDS-EL w/o TPS Ablation This work KDS-EL w/o TPS&KER Ablation This work MEL Baseline [12] FWPSO Single-objective [8] PSO-CSM Single-objective [11] 5.1. Experimental Setup SaWDE Single-objective [9] This section details the experimental framework. The evaluation employs 20 benchmark datasets drawn from five domains: 15 gene expression microar- rays (ALL1, ALL4, ALL_AML, Adenoma, Colon, DLBCL, Gastric, Gastric1, Gastric2, Leukaemia, Lymphoma, Myeloma, Prostate, SRBCT, and T1D), two text corpora (BASEHOCK and PCMAC), one image dataset (COIL20), one speech dataset (ISOLET), and one synthetic dataset (madelon). Table 2 summa- rizes their key characteristics. The datasets span feature dimensionalities from 500 (madelon) to 54,675 (T1D) and sample sizes from 36 (Adenoma) to 2,600 (madelon), capturing the hallmark p ≫ n configuration: 17 of 20 datasets pos- sess more features than instances. Class structure ranges from 17 binary prob- lems to SRBCT (4 classes), COIL20 (20), and ISOLET (26). The collection was selected to span low-, medium-, and ultra-high-dimensional regimes and to in- clude eight gene-expression datasets—ALL1, ALL_AML, Adenoma, DLBCL, Gastric2, Leukaemia, Lymphoma, and SRBCT—on which methods routinely reach near-perfect accuracy (above 0.998). On these ceiling datasets accuracy alone ceases to discriminate among methods, so the number of selected features becomes the decisive metric; Section 5.5 pursues this evaluation. Fourteen fixed-length feature selection methods are compared, organized into three groups. The first comprises the complete KDS-EL and the config- urations obtained by successively removing its mechanisms, where TPS de- notes Two-Phase Weight Scheduling: KDS-EL w/o TPS (without Two-Phase scheduling), KDS-EL w/o TPS&KER (additionally without the KER strategy), and MEL [12]—which constitute the ablation chain analyzed in Section 5.8. The second consists of five single-objective evolutionary methods: FWPSO [8], PSO-CSM [11], SaWDE [9], IGPSO [10], and the classic BPSO [7]. The third IGPSO Single-objective [10] BPSO Single-objective [7] W-MOPSO-FS Multi-objective Self-built fMOPSO-FS Multi-objective [51] NSGA-II-FS Multi-objective [32] MOEA-D-FS Multi-objective [33] MOPSO-FS Multi-objective [34] This section reports the experimental outcomes across six complementary perspectives: overall classification accuracy, feature-selection compactness, sta- tistical significance, ceiling-effect behavior, convergence dynamics, and com- putational efficiency. All aggregate numbers are computed over the 20 bench- mark datasets described in Section 5.1. We then quantify the contribution of each mechanism in Section 5.8 and assess the sensitivity of KDS-EL to its hyper-parameters in Section 5.9. 5.2. Overall Classification Accuracy Table 4 presents per-dataset and aggregate accuracy of the 14 methods. KDS-EL ranks first with a mean of 0.9574, leading KDS-EL w/o TPS by +0.86 pp, the strongest single-objective competitor FWPSO [8] by +3.97 pp, and the strongest multi-objective competitor W-MOPSO-FS by +4.42 pp. Against MEL [12]—the framework stripped of all three mechanisms—the margin is +7.06 pp. The per-cell symbols in Table 4 make the comparison structure explicit: KDS-EL is significantly better than every competitor on at least 14 of the 20 datasets. The ≈ ties concentrate on ceiling-effect gene-expression problems and on the strongest ablation variant (KDS-EL w/o TPS), while the only − en- tries occur against multi-objective methods on ALL1, COIL20, SRBCT, BASE- HOCK, and ISOLET, where those methods reach perfect or highest accuracy at the cost of substantially larger feature subsets, as detailed in Section 5.3. 7 BASEHOCK, COIL20, and ISOLET, NSGA-II-FS [32] attains the highest accuracy (0.9238, 0.9971, and 0.9090 versus 0.9113, 0.9939, and 0.8894 for KDS-EL); these moderate-dimensionality, larger-sample problems favor non-dominated-sorting methods, which retain a structural advantage at the cost of 2,073, 283, and 185 features respectively—several times to an order of magnitude more than KDS-EL, as detailed in Section 5.3. KDS-EL also exhibits narrower accuracy dispersion across runs, as the standard deviations in Table 4 indicate, showing that MI-guided initialization and KER refinement suppress run-to-run variance alongside raising central tendency; its advantage is consistent rather than the artifact of a few lucky runs. Feature-Selection Compactness KDS-EL selects, on average, 87.8 features across the 20-dataset bench- mark, corresponding to an effective selection ratio of approximately 2–3%. For comparison, MEL retains 2,722 features, and all multi-objective meth- ods (W-MOPSO-FS, fMOPSO-FS, NSGA-II-FS, MOEA-D-FS, MOPSO-FS) select between 2,960 and 5,263 features on average. Even the most compact single-objective competitor, FWPSO, selects 1,069 features—more than an or- der of magnitude above KDS-EL. Table 5 reports the per-dataset feature counts, and Fig. 4 reports the per-dataset selection ratio of all 14 methods on a log scale, underscoring the consistent compactness of KDS-EL relative to every competi- tor. This combined finding—equal or higher accuracy with 20- to 50-fold compression—has a clear Pareto interpretation: in the accuracy-versus-features plane, KDS-EL occupies the extreme top-left region no competing method can dominate. The compression is most pronounced on gene-expression data: on ALL1, 0.9998 accuracy with 39 features (0.31% of 12,625) versus 4,248 for MEL; on Gastric1 (22,283 dimensions), 0.9800 with 31 features (0.14%) versus 6,044 for the most compact multi-objective method; on Colon, 14 features—a 140:1 compression—at the highest accuracy (0.9500); on Prostate, 26 features at 0.9701. Across all 20 datasets the feature count ascends monotonically along the ablation chain: 87.8 (KDS-EL) → 122 (KDS-EL w/o TPS) → 291 (KDS-EL w/o TPS&KER) → 2,722 (MEL). These figures illustrate KDS-EL’s central empirical contribution: diagnostic-quality classification on high-dimensional biomedical data using a fraction of the original feature budget. Statistical Significance The ranking is underpinned by the Demšar [52] framework for classifier comparison over multiple datasets. Pairwise Wilcoxon tests. One-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank tests (p < 0.05) in the direction of superiority confirm that KDS-EL significantly outperforms MEL, PSO-CSM, IGPSO, and BPSO on all 20 datasets (20/20); KDS-EL w/o TPS&KER, FWPSO, and SaWDE on 19/20; KDS-EL w/o TPS on 13/20; and the five multi-objective methods on 14–18 of 20. We adopt the one-sided formulation because each comparison tests the explicit claim that the row method outperforms the column method, following the Demšar [52] protocol for superiority claims. The lower counts against MOFS-class methods (14 vs. W-MOPSO-FS, 15 vs. fMOPSO-FS, 16 vs. NSGA-II-FS and MOEA-D-FS) do not imply weaker performance: they reflect ceiling-effect datasets where accuracy is saturated and statistical ties prevail, while KDS-EL decisively dominates on feature count, as discussed in Section 5.5. Table 6 reports the pairwise win counts, confirming that no competitor outperforms KDS-EL on a majority of datasets. Table 4 provides the complementary per-dataset view: its +, ≈, and − sym- bols come from two-sided rank-sum tests within each dataset, whereas Table 6 pools one-sided signed-rank tests across datasets. Both protocols agree that no competitor holds a significant advantage over KDS-EL on a majority of datasets. Holm-Bonferroni correction. Table 7 presents the Holm-Bonferroni step- down correction [54] applied to the 13 pairwise comparisons between KDS-EL and every other method. All 13 null hypotheses of no superiority are rejected at corrected significance levels; the one-sided Wilcoxon p-values are so small that both the Fisher combined p-values and the Holm-adjusted p-values are below 10 −15 and are reported as such in Table 7. Even the most conservative compar- ison, against KDS-EL w/o TPS, rejects H 0 at α = 0.05. These results confirm that removing any individual component yields a statistically significant degra- dation in accuracy, consistent with the component-wise analysis of Section 5.8. The complete method therefore holds the best Friedman rank, while the pairwise Wilcoxon and Holm-Bonferroni tests in Ta- bles 6 and 7 establish significance over all 13 competitors. Convergence Behavior 5.90 fMOPSO-FS 6.20 FWPSO Fig. 6 shows the mean convergence trajectories of KDS-EL, KDS-EL w/o TPS, KDS-EL w/o TPS&KER, and MEL averaged over the 20 datasets. KDS- EL enters the high-accuracy region within the first 10–15 iterations thanks to MI-guided initialization, and KER then drives a prolonged refinement that lifts accuracy past iteration 30 where competitors have plateaued. The Two-Phase schedule yields a characteristic “fast-drop → plateau → micro-rise” trajectory: after aggressive feature reduction under Phase 1 weights, accuracy plateaus un- til the Phase 2 switch triggers a final upward correction, whereas KDS-EL w/o TPS plateaus earlier at lower terminal accuracy. MEL, initialized randomly, needs 40–60 iterations to exit the low-accuracy regime; MOFS-class methods stagnate late because Pareto-front maintenance retains a diverse archive that dilutes search pressure, flattening their curves after iteration 60. 6.95 NSGA-II-FS MOEA-D-FS 7.75 MOPSO-FS 7.80 8.60 PSO-CSM 9.45 SaWDE MEL 11.65 IGPSO 11.70 13.35 BPSO 0 2 4 6 8 10 Average Friedman Rank (lower = better) 12 14 Figure 5: Average Friedman ranks of the 14 methods over the 20-dataset accuracy matrix (lower is better), computed from the same per-dataset mean accuracies used in Table 4. 5.5. Ceiling-Effect Analysis on Gene-Expression Data 5.7. Computational Efficiency Eight datasets in the benchmark—ALL1, ALL_AML, Adenoma, DLBCL, Gastric2, Leukaemia, Lymphoma, and SRBCT—exhibit mean accuracy at or above 0.998 across the top-performing methods. On these datasets, the accu- racy differences among the leading methods are typically narrower than 0.002, which corresponds to at most one or two misclassified instances across ten in- dependent five-fold cross-validation runs. At this saturation level, classification accuracy ceases to be a meaningful discriminator; instead, the number of fea- tures selected becomes the primary figure of merit. KDS-EL selects between 39 (ALL1) and 83 (Gastric2) features across these eight datasets. In contrast, the best single-objective competitor, FWPSO, retains 278–1,362 features, and the multi-objective methods select between 700 and 10,701 features on the same data. This gap carries practical significance for gene-expression analysis: a compact signature of 40–80 genes is amenable to targeted biological validation, pathway enrichment analysis, and potential clin- ical deployment, whereas signatures spanning several hundred to several thou- sand genes offer little interpretability and are vulnerable to overfitting in the p ≫ n regime. That KDS-EL ties or marginally trails methods achieving perfect 1.0 on ALL1 and SRBCT does not indicate inferior discrimination: all methods mis- classify fewer than two samples on average, differing only in which samples are misclassified—stochastic variation expected in small-sample data. A simi- lar pattern holds on Lymphoma (45 samples), where KDS-EL and KDS-EL w/o TPS share the best accuracy of 0.9994 with a difference of zero, yet KDS-EL achieves this with 45 features versus 1,027 for W-MOPSO-FS. We therefore KDS-EL records a mean runtime of 51.4 seconds, ranking second among all methods and trailing FWPSO by only 1.7 seconds (49.7 s). Relative to MEL (175.0 s), KDS-EL achieves a 3.4× speedup. All five multi-objective methods exceed 110 seconds on average—more than double the runtime of KDS-EL— owing to the overhead of non-dominated sorting and Pareto-archive mainte- nance at each generation. KDS-EL thereby occupies the high-accuracy, low- runtime corner of the accuracy–runtime trade-off; the complete per-dataset run- time table is provided in the Supplementary Material. The efficiency advantage is most pronounced at high dimensionality: on T1D (54,675 features) KDS-EL finishes in 118.8 s versus 256.6 s for PSO- CSM (2.2×), and on BASEHOCK it is 4.7× faster than SaWDE (130.1 s vs. 616.0 s). Three factors explain this: MI-guided initialization shortens the path to a high-quality region; KER refines elites within a bounded refinement bud- get that does not alter the dominant per-iteration complexity; and Two-Phase scheduling concentrates feature reduction early so search later operates on com- pact, cheaper subsets. FWPSO’s marginal 1.7 s lead stems from its SA-driven local search, which terminates early on small-sample problems at the expense of a 3.97-percentage-point accuracy deficit. 5.8. Component Contribution Analysis 5.8.1. Aggregate Contributions The ablation chain follows a remove-in-sequence paradigm and reads sub- tractively: each row of Table 8 strips one mechanism from the complete KDS- EL (0.9574 accuracy, 87.8 features on average), and the accuracy loss at each 9 (a) Mean Convergence (averaged over 20 datasets) 0.95 0.90 0.85 0.80 0.75 KDS-EL KDS-EL w/o TPS 0 20 40 (b) Adenoma (36×7457) (c) DLBCL (77×7129) 0.96 0.97 Accuracy Accuracy Accuracy 0.97 0.96 0.95 0.78 0.75 0.95 0.94 0.94 0.93 0.70 20 40 60 Iteration 80 100 0.92 0.90 0.80 0.73 0 (e) BASEHOCK (1993×4862) 0.83 0.98 0.98 20 40 60 Iteration 80 100 0.88 0.86 0.84 0.82 0.68 0 100 0.92 0.85 0.99 0.99 KDS-EL w/o TPS&KER MEL 80 (d) T1D (101×54675) 0.88 1.00 1.00 60 Iteration Accuracy Mean Accuracy (20 DS) 1.00 0 20 40 60 Iteration 80 100 0 20 40 60 Iteration 80 100 Figure 6: Mean convergence trajectories of KDS-EL, KDS-EL w/o TPS, KDS-EL w/o TPS&KER, and MEL averaged over the 20 benchmark datasets. step quantifies the removed component’s contribution. These four configura- tions are exactly the methods compared in Section 5: KDS-EL w/o TPS is KDS-EL without Two-Phase scheduling, KDS-EL w/o TPS&KER is KDS-EL without both the KER strategy and Two-Phase scheduling, and MEL [12] is the framework stripped of all three mechanisms—the residual that remains once every component has been removed. Removing MI-guided initialization and adaptive re-initialization inflicts the largest single accuracy loss: -4.58pp, dropping the mean accuracy from 0.9325 to 0.8868 while the feature count expands from 291 to 2,722, roughly an order of magnitude. This dominant role stems from informed starting posi- tions and stagnation-triggered re-initialization: the MI-informed half provides a high-quality search origin, while adaptive re-initialization counters premature convergence. Removing the KER strategy costs a further -1.63pp, dropping the mean accuracy from 0.9488 to 0.9325 and expanding the feature set from 122 to 291. Because the accumulated importance matrix is derived from fitness com- parisons already performed during search, KER’s contribution is obtained at a bounded refinement cost that does not alter the dominant per-iteration com- plexity; this gain is also achieved on top of the importance-matrix knowledge already present in MEL, confirming that KER re-deploys rather than duplicates it. Removing the Two-Phase Weight Scheduling strategy from the complete KDS-EL costs -0.86pp, dropping the mean accuracy from 0.9574 to 0.9488 and expanding the feature set from 87.8 to 122. Runtime also rises from 51.4 s to 53.6 s during this removal. Each component contributes along a distinct dimension of the search pro- cess, and its removal damages that dimension. MI-guided initialization operates in the start-and-reduction dimension, providing the bulk of feature reduction alongside an informed search origin. The KER strategy occupies the accuracy dimension, refining elite solutions through cross-iteration accumulated knowl- edge at a bounded refinement cost. The Two-Phase strategy delivers simultane- ous gains across all three axes—accuracy, sparsity, and efficiency—by aligning objective weights with the structural phases of the search. The mechanisms are complementary and independent—none subsumes another, and each is verifi- able in isolation. 4248 features at 0.9664. On Adenoma, MEL selects 2483 features at 0.9410 accuracy, KDS-EL w/o TPS&KER compresses to 120 at 0.9958, KDS-EL w/o TPS to 33, and the complete KDS-EL to 66, with the latter two tying at the saturated accuracy of 0.9996. DLBCL, Leukaemia, Lymphoma, and SRBCT follow the same trajectory: accuracy saturates early, and the configurations differentiate through increasingly compact feature subsets with no accuracy penalty. On medium-difficulty datasets, accuracy degrades in a stair-step progres- sion as mechanisms are removed. On BASEHOCK, the accuracy sequence reads 0.9113 (KDS-EL), 0.8997 (KDS-EL w/o TPS), 0.8597 (KDS-EL w/o TPS&KER), and 0.8518 (MEL). On madelon, a comparable trajectory emerges: 0.8822, 0.8659, 0.7679, and 0.7521. The sharpest feature inflation uniformly occurs when MI-guided initialization is removed (the KDS-EL w/o TPS&KER- to-MEL step), where feature counts expand by an order of magnitude on most high-dimensional gene-expression datasets. On Gastric1, features rise from 678 to 7,393; on T1D, from 174 to 6,715; on Prostate, from 27 to 5,058. These pat- terns confirm that the initial investment in MI-informed initialization delivers both the dominant accuracy contribution and the foundational feature reduction on which subsequent mechanisms build. 5.8.3. Two-Phase Scheduling and In-place Update Verification The Two-Phase Weight Scheduling strategy is isolated by comparing the complete KDS-EL against its fixed-weight counterpart (fixed ws=[0.9, 0.1] with in-place update) on the same 20-dataset batch. Removing the schedule lowers accuracy from 0.9574 to 0.9488 (-0.86pp), expands average features from 87.8 to 122, and increases runtime from 51.4 s to 53.6 s. Following the Phase-2 weight switch in the full method, accuracy continues to rise while features undergo further compression, confirming that the coarse-then-fine schedule outperforms a fixed-weight regime. On a per-dataset basis, Table 4 shows that KDS-EL is not inferior to the fixed-weight configuration on the overwhelming majority of datasets. 5.9. Parameter Sensitivity Analysis To assess the sensitivity of KDS-EL to its key hyper-parameters, we conduct a one-factor-at-a-time analysis on four representative datasets: Adenoma (36 samples, 7,457 features), Colon (62, 2,000), ALL4 (93, 12,625), and BASEHOCK (1,993, 4,862). The subset spans small-sample gene expression and larger-sample text domains, with 2,000–12,625 features. Five parameters—WeightDecay, PhaseSplit, flip_frac, MI_init_ratio, and elite_k— are varied individually while the remaining four stay fixed at their defaults listed in Table 3. For each configuration, the mean accuracy, feature count, and runtime across the four datasets are recorded; Table 9 summarizes the tested ranges, optimal values, stable bands, and maximum accuracy deviations, and the complete tables are provided in the Supplementary Material. Across all five parameters, the maximum accuracy deviation from the default configuration never exceeds ±1.5 pp. Weight decay (WeightDecay). This parameter controls the discounting rate of historical feature importance scores. At the default 0.99, the four-dataset mean is 0.944 accuracy, 107 features, and 51.3 s. Reducing the decay to 0.90 erodes accuracy to 0.932 (−1.2 pp), as the importance matrix forgets useful patterns too rapidly. Disabling decay (1.00) inflates the feature count by ap- proximately 40% (to 151) with no accuracy benefit—stale scores accumulate without bound. Performance plateaus across [0.95, 0.995], with accuracy fluc- tuation under ±1.2 pp. Phase split ratio (PhaseSplit). This parameter governs the proportion of iterations allocated to aggressive feature reduction before accuracy-oriented re- finement. The default 0.70 gives 70% of iterations to Phase 1. Values below 0.50 yield insufficient reduction time, leaving elevated feature counts (146– 189), while 0.90 starves the refinement phase and reduces accuracy by 0.7 pp. The stable band [0.60, 0.80] keeps variation below 0.5 pp, confirming the sched- ule tolerates imprecise split points. Elite flip fraction (flip_frac). At the default 0.01, roughly one feature per 100 dimensions is flipped per elite. Reducing this to 0.005 slows convergence (runtime +3.5 s). Increasing it beyond 0.02 injects excessive randomness: at 0.10, accuracy drops by 1.3 pp and features nearly double (to 203), indicat- ing random perturbation overwhelms knowledge-guided refinement. Only the narrow window [0.005, 0.02] preserves the intended knowledge–randomness balance. MI initialization ratio (MI_init_ratio). This is the most influential pa- rameter. At the default 0.50, half the population is seeded with MI-ranked fea- tures. Eliminating MI guidance (0.00) imposes a cold start—accuracy falls by 1.2 pp and runtime rises by 21% (to 62.3 s) as the search rediscovers informative features from scratch. Full MI initialization (1.00) causes premature conver- gence (−0.8 pp) through reduced diversity. The stable band [0.25, 0.75] keeps accuracy within 0.4 pp of the optimum. Elite count (elite_k). With N = 20, the default of three elites represents 15% of the swarm. A single elite restricts knowledge propagation (0.938 accu- racy), while 10 elites dilute the quality signal of the KER strategy (0.935 ac- curacy, 141 features). The stable range [2, 5] maintains accuracy within 0.3 pp of the optimum, confirming that a moderate elite subset concentrates computa- tional effort on the most promising candidates without dilution. The defaults therefore transfer directly to new datasets without per-dataset tuning; practitioners should preserve MI_init_ratio and flip_frac, which exhibit the largest individual sensitivity and jointly govern the balance between injected prior knowledge and exploratory diversity. — 0/20 0/20 0/20 0/20 0/20 0/20 0/20 0/20 0/20 0/20 0/20 0/20 0/20 KDS-EL Method Table 8: Component contribution analysis: each row strips one mechanism from the complete KDS-EL, and ∆Acc reports the resulting accuracy loss relative to the row above. “MEL” denotes the framework stripped of all three mechanisms—the residual that remains once every component has been removed, corresponding to MEL [12]. Conclusion This paper presented KDS-EL, a closed-loop knowledge-guided evolu- tionary framework addressing three structural limitations of general-purpose PSO in high-dimensional feature selection: random initialization provides insufficient guidance in sparse high-dimensional spaces, uniform mutation discards cross-iteration feature-importance signals, and static objective prefer- ences cannot adapt to different evolutionary phases. MI-guided initialization and adaptive re-initialization supply informed starting points and stagnation es- cape; removing them costs the largest single loss of 4.58pp and lets the feature set expand from 291 to 2,722. The KER strategy accumulates cross-iteration feature-importance scores from fitness comparisons already performed during search and conducts knowledge-guided elite flipping with a bounded refinement budget; removing it costs a further 1.63pp and expands the feature set from 122 to 291. Two-Phase Weight Scheduling aligns objective weights with search phases—aggressive feature reduction followed by accuracy refinement; removing it costs 0.86pp and expands the feature set from 87.8 to 122. On 20 high-dimensional datasets spanning gene expression, text, image, and speech domains, KDS-EL ranks first among 14 fixed-length methods, surpassing the strongest single-objective and multi-objective competitors by +3.97pp and +4.42pp. Wilcoxon tests confirm superiority over MEL in 20/20 datasets; Holm-Bonferroni correction establishes significance against all 13 competitors. KDS-EL delivers a 3.4× speedup over MEL (51.4 s vs. 175.0 s) with parameter sensitivity within ±1.5pp. Several limitations suggest future directions. MI-based feature ranking in- curs O(D log D) preprocessing cost, a bottleneck when D exceeds 10 5 , where GPU-accelerated MI estimation may be required. The method currently tar- gets single-label classification; extensions to multi-label learning, streaming feature selection, class-imbalanced data, and deep embedding representations remain open. Promising directions include GPU-accelerated MI approximation, multi-label and imbalanced extensions, transformer-based feature representa- tions, and cross-dataset transfer via multi-task evolutionary extensions of the proposed framework.
